Stabilizing Datasets

stabilizing-datasets.Rmd

From noisy to stable

Real data arrives in whatever form it was entered: dates as 03/15/2019 or 15-Mar-2019, booleans as Y/yes/TRUE/1, dollars as $1,200, ZIP codes that a spreadsheet already mangled into 6037. A stabilized dataset is the same data rewritten into a canonical form that behaves — one that the next program reads correctly instead of guessing.

stabilize_data() applies the DGF’s rules to a raw extract and returns that clean version, which write_stable_csv() writes as a governed CSV carrying its own DGF and provenance.

stable <- stabilize_data(raw_data, dgf, use_v7 = TRUE)
write_stable_csv(stable, "data-governed.csv", dgf = dgf)

Two outcomes: stabilized to type, or stabilized safely

Not every column can be losslessly typed in a CSV — and datagoodr is careful about the difference.

Stabilized to type

Columns whose meaning a reader can recover are converted to a canonical form that imports to the right type:

kind raw stabilized imports as
calendar date 03/15/2019, 15-Mar-2019 2019-03-15 a date
boolean Y, yes, 1 TRUE logical
currency $1,200.00 1200.00 a number
compact month 201903 2019-03 a month

These are the satisfying cases: the stabilized column reloads as exactly the type it should be, in every tool, without further instruction.

Stabilized safely

Some distinctions a plain CSV simply cannot carry — a factor’s levels, an identifier’s identity. Forcing them would lose information, so datagoodr protects the column instead of converting it. The guiding rule is: never import in a way that loses data.

  • Factors default to text. A categorical column is kept as its written values rather than silently re-coded to integers, so the labels survive. You add the meaning (levels, definitions) in the DGF; see Documenting Data.
  • Identifiers are protected, not parsed. A ZIP or FIPS or EIN keeps its exact written form — 06037 stays 06037, never 6037; a long ID is not cast to a lossy double.

“Safe” means that even when datagoodr cannot promote a column to a richer type, the governed CSV never imports it in a way that corrupts or drops information.

The guard that makes “safe” real

The danger is a confident but wrong conversion. A column of ZIP codes looks exactly like a number, and a naive reader would type it as one — turning 06037 into 6037. datagoodr’s storage-safety gate refuses to let any numeric stabilization re-type a column whose values carry leading zeros or exceed the range integers can represent exactly. One rule protects every FIPS, ZIP, EIN, and NAICS column at once, in both directions: if a column cannot safely become a number, nothing may make it one.

See the effect before you commit

A stabilization rule is only as good as its fit to the data. When the DGF proposes a stabilizer, it previews the result on the first few values in stable_first5, so a mis-detected date order (parsing 03/04/2019 as April 3 instead of March 4) is visible on sight rather than discovered downstream. A reformat the system cannot perform — say converting a fiscal year to a calendar year with no conversion defined — is reported as not transformable rather than guessed. (The rule machinery is the read :: [convert] :: write plan from the companion package formex; see Guessing Data Types for how the pieces are chosen.)
